jina.title: Understanding Fiscal Years and Fiscal Periods // Accounting & Fiscal Services // UC Irvine
jina.snippet:
A fiscal year is important for accounting purposes and for preparing annual financial statements. At UC Irvine, the fiscal year begins on July 1 and ends on June 30. Because the fiscal year straddles two different calendar years, the calendar year and fiscal year will not always match. For example, Fiscal Year 2027 runs from July 1, 2026 – June 30, 2027. Each fiscal year is further broken down into segments called "fiscal periods."

## Fiscal Periods

There are a total of 15 fiscal periods to which General Ledger entries can be posted. Twelve of these periods simply represent the 12 months of the year, but three other special periods exist: Beginning Balances (BB), C&G Beginning Balances (CB), and Period 13.

Most fiscal periods — except for special periods like BB and CB — include five working days after the calendar month has ended. During these five days, some (but not all) transactions can be posted to the closing period. jina.snippet:
In Brief

Although many businesses operate on a fiscal year distinct from the calendar year, some use a distinctive 52/53-week fiscal year. This reporting convention can enhance the comparability of periods and the convenience of reporting timeframes, but it also comes with disadvantages and may not be fully understood by market participants. This article reviews the use of the 52/53-week convention of the past several decades and notes that although its use may be declining overall, it remains popular in certain industries.

Hire Accountants

***

[Accounting](https://www.cpajournal.com/2022/03/16/how-long-is-a-year/#) professionals are well aware that companies have choices about how to define a fiscal year. After all, many businesses operate on a fiscal year that does not coincide with the calendar year. In some industries, a variation of the fiscal year concept known as the 52/53-week fiscal year is also common. In fact, the National Retail Federation encourages the use of a 52/53-week fiscal year, also known as the 4-5-4 calendar ([https://bit.ly/3GqbUfx](https://bit.ly/3GqbUfx)). The basic idea of this calendar is to think in terms of 52 weeks rather than 12 months. #### Accounting Periods

You must use a tax year to figure your taxable income. A tax year is an annual accounting period for keeping records and reporting income and expenses. An annual accounting period does not include a short tax year (discussed later). You can use the following tax years:

* A calendar year; or
* A fiscal year (including a 52-53-week tax year).

Unless you have a required tax year, you adopt a tax year by filing your first income tax return using that tax year. A required tax year is a tax year required under the Internal Revenue Code or the Treasury Regulations. You cannot adopt a tax year by merely:

* Filing an application for an extension of time to file an income tax return;
* Filing an application for an employer identification number (Form SS-4); or
* Paying estimated taxes.

This section discusses:

* A calendar year.
* A fiscal year (including a period of 52 or 53 weeks).

...

Generally, anyone can adopt the calendar year. However, you must adopt the calendar year if:

* You keep no books or records;
* You have no annual accounting period;
* Your present tax year does not qualify as a fiscal year; or
* You are required to use a calendar year by a provision in the Internal Revenue Code or Treasury Regulations.

#### Fiscal Year

A fiscal year is 12 consecutive months ending on the last day of any month except December 31st. If you are allowed to adopt a fiscal year, you must consistently maintain your books and records and report your income and expenses using the time period adopted.

seltz.snippet:
A nonprofit fiscal year is the 12-month accounting period an organization uses for its budget, financial statements, and federal tax filings. Federal rules let you pick any 12-month cycle that fits how you actually operate, not just January through December. That choice sets your Form 990 due date, your audit timing, and the rhythm of your board and grant reporting for as long as the organization exists, so it’s worth getting right on day one.

## What Counts as a Fiscal Year

A calendar year runs January 1 through December 31. A fiscal year is any 12-month period ending on the last day of a month other than December. Federal regulations also allow a 52–53 week fiscal year that always ends on the same day of the week, such as the last Saturday in June, and doesn’t have to land on the final day of a month. All three are valid tax years, provided the organization keeps its books consistently within the period it chose.

The distinction drives real dates. A calendar-year nonprofit files Form 990 by May 15. A nonprofit with a June 30 year-end files by November 15. Pick the wrong period and your finance staff will be closing the books during the same weeks they’re delivering your biggest programs.

## How to Choose a Fiscal Year That Fits Your Operations

The best fiscal year usually ends after your peak activity winds down, not in the middle of it. That gives staff room to close the books, reconcile grants, and prepare reports without competing against program delivery.

seltz.title: Fiscal Year Definition, and How It Differs From Tax Year
seltz.snippet:
A fiscal year is an annual accounting period of 12 consecutive months ending on the last day of any month other than December, or a 52-53-week taxable year the taxpayer has elected, an annual accounting period being the period on the basis of which a taxpayer regularly computes its income in keeping its books (26 CFR 1.441-1(b)(3) and 1.441-1(b)(5)(i)). The alternative is a calendar year, the 12-month period ending December 31, and the Internal Revenue Code defines each as a period of 12 months, separated by that December ending (26 U.S.C. 441(d) and 441(e)). The label is conditional on the books, because a fiscal year is recognized only if the taxpayer’s books are kept in accordance with it (26 CFR 1.441-1(b)(5)(ii)).

## The 52-53-Week Fiscal Year

A taxpayer that regularly computes income on an annual period varying from 52 to 53 weeks, always ending on the same day of the week, may elect to use it. The period has to end on whatever date that day last occurs in a calendar month, or on whatever date it falls nearest to the last day of a calendar month, and once elected it is what fiscal year means for that taxpayer (26 U.S.C. 441(e) and 441(f)(1)).

The two endings behave differently, which a close calendar has to account for. Under the last-occurs rule the year always ends inside the month, on the last day or as many as six days before it. Under the nearest rule it may end on the last day, or as many as three days before or after it, so a year keyed to that rule can close in the following calendar month (26 CFR 1.441-2(a)(2)).

you.snippet:
A fiscal year is a twelve month period used by businesses and governments for budgeting and financial reporting. A fiscal year is a 12-month period used for accounting that doesn't necessarily align with the calendar year.
A fiscal year is a 12-month period used for accounting, financial reporting, and budgeting. Unlike a calendar year, which runs from January through December, a fiscal year can begin and end in any month depending on the organization. The U.S. federal government’s fiscal year starts in October, while many retail businesses choose a fiscal year that matches their sales cycles.
The designation of fiscal years typically includes the 365 days in which most of the period falls. For example, a company’s Fiscal Year 2025 (often abbreviated as FY2025 or FY25) may run from Feb. 1, 2025, to Jan. 31, 2026. This naming convention helps maintain clarity and consistency in financial communications and reporting. While many fiscal years begin from the first of a particular month, they can also begin at other dates, such as during the middle of the month.
Organizations can defer income recognition by choosing a fiscal year that ends before their peak revenue period. For example, a construction company might choose a March 31 fiscal year-end if most of its contracts are finished during the summer months, effectively postponing income recognition and hence the related tax liability.
